items.q: What is Base?
items.a: Base is a power company in Texas and Illinois. It puts a large backup battery at your home. In some areas it is also your electricity provider. Base says 30,000+ homes use it.

items.q: How does sign-up work?
items.a: Three steps on Base's page. 1: check your zip or talk to an energy advisor. 2: Base engineers review your setup and say if the home fits, and for 0, 1 or 2 batteries. 3: install in two visits.
items.source: Base How it works page, paraphrased (faq/corpus/how-it-works.md)

items.q: What plans are there?
items.a: Three on Base's page. Energy: a fixed rate, where you can choose your provider. Backup + Energy: the battery plus energy. Backup Only: the battery with your current utility, in some areas only.
items.source: Base home page and pricing page (faq/corpus/home.md, pricing.md)

items.q: What does it cost?
items.a: It depends on your address. Base's sample plan for Oncor areas is a $695 one-time install, a $19 monthly membership and an all-in rate of 13.9 cents per kWh. Enter your zip on Base's site for your price.

items.q: Do I have to switch my electricity provider?
items.a: Not always. It depends on who delivers your power. In co-op and city utility areas (Austin Energy is one), your utility stays and Base adds only the battery.

items.q: What do I need to do?
items.a: Check 5 short answers about your home, then add one photo of your panel if you can. City permits fill in most of it first; you only confirm or correct.
items.source: The My Home steps. Each answer starts from the city permit record for the home.
items.computed: web/onboarding.js ORDER (the questions) and the photo task

items.q: How long does the install take?
items.a: Two visits. The first puts in the electrical equipment. Base comes back within three weeks to put the battery outside near your meter. No one needs to be home, and your power stays on.

items.q: Where does the battery go?
items.a: Outside, near your electric meter. Base says it finds a clean, code-compliant spot close to the meter, and adds a soft start for a large air conditioner if needed.
items.source: Base How it works page, quoted (faq/corpus/how-it-works.md)

items.q: Why might my wall not fit?
items.a: Our rule of thumb, from installer reports: a battery needs about 9 ft of clear outside wall, and 3 ft from the gas meter, the A/C unit and the fence. This is our estimate, not Base's rule. A Base engineer makes the real check.

items.q: What would make my home a yes?
items.a: Usually one or two steps. The most common reason in our sample is: existing solar or battery on the permit record. The fix is a photo of the label and the panel, then an engineer check. Each step says who does it and if it needs a permit.
items.number: 11 of 18 sample homes share that reason
items.source: Sample homes in 78745 and the fit rules. Costs are not estimated.
items.label: Sample homes, not your home

items.q: How big is the battery?
items.a: 39.2 kWh in each Base Core. Base says that is one of the largest home batteries.

items.q: What will my battery do today?
items.a: On 2026-09-26 the plan is to charge from 8 am to 11 am, when power is cheapest, and send power back from 6 pm to 9 pm, when it is dearest. 30% of the 39.2 kWh always stays in for your backup.
items.number: Net $0.95 for the day on one battery (LZ_AEN)
items.source: Today's ERCOT day-ahead prices for the Austin zone, one charge and one discharge a day. Our plan, not Base's real dispatch.
items.computed: web/data/grid_today.json battery (built by grid/today.py from the ERCOT system-wide-prices feed)
items.label: Our model, not Base's dispatch

items.q: Why is my battery not full?
items.a: That is expected. The battery charges when power is cheap and may send some back when the grid is stressed. Base always keeps backup in reserve, and the charge rarely drops to that minimum.
items.number: 30% kept for backup in our plan
items.source: Base How it works page (faq/corpus/how-it-works.md); 30% is our plan in grid/earned.py

items.q: What did one battery earn last year?
items.a: About $603 for all of 2025, or $1.65 a day, on real Austin prices. This is a floor: day-ahead prices and one cycle a day only. It is the value to the grid, not a payment to you.
items.source: ERCOT day-ahead price archive (report 13060), Austin zone, 39.2 kWh battery, 30% kept for backup.
items.label: Our estimate, not a Base offer

items.q: When is the grid most stressed?
items.a: Late afternoon and evening. Texas uses the most power from 5 pm to 6 pm, and Austin prices are highest from 6 pm to 10 pm. Solar fades then while air conditioning is still on.
items.number: Peak load hour ends 6 pm (63,116 MW average); top price hours 6 pm to 10 pm
items.source: ERCOT hourly load 2024-01-01 to 2026-08-31 and day-ahead prices for the Austin zone.
items.computed: SELECT he, AVG(ercot) FROM load_hourly GROUP BY he; SELECT he, AVG(price) FROM dam_prices WHERE point='LZ_AEN' GROUP BY he

items.q: How does Base keep rates low?
items.a: Base says: we earn from the grid, not you. The battery helps balance the grid at peak demand.

items.q: Is the battery safe?
items.a: Base says the battery is certified to UL 1973, UL 1741, UL 9540 and UL 9540A. It is tested from -22 to 122 F, for flash floods, and under 3 ft of water.
items.source: Base home and How it works pages (faq/corpus/home.md, how-it-works.md)

items.q: What happens when the power goes out?
items.a: The battery takes over by itself, usually in under half a second. Base says most members do not notice.
items.source: Base How it works and home pages (faq/corpus/how-it-works.md, home.md)

items.q: How long does backup last?
items.a: Up to 36 hours on one battery, and about 36 to 72 hours with 1 or 2. It depends on how much power you use.
items.source: Base home and How it works pages

items.q: What if the outage lasts longer than the battery?
items.a: Base's page says you can recharge the battery with a generator through the built-in port, or with connected solar. Neither is required.

items.q: Why did my battery not turn on?
items.a: The home must use under 20 kW for the battery to start. If large devices push use higher, turn some off, then turn the battery on in the Base App.

items.q: What is the clearance rule?
items.a: About 9 ft of clear outside wall per battery, next to the electric meter and main panel, with 3 ft from the gas meter, 3 ft from the A/C condenser and 3 ft from the fence. A rule-only estimate for triage, not a site plan.

items.a: Four reasons in the rule: the usable wall is under 9 ft; the lot is under 4,500 sq ft with a detached garage (unclear, send a tech); the house covers over 40% of the lot, so the side yard is thin; or gas is unknown, so the rule keeps 3 ft clear for a meter that may exist.

items.q: What does the base week signal mean?
items.a: Base week: are Base permits up or down against the last 4 weeks? Rule: Base permits issued in the last 7 days vs the mean of the 4 prior weeks. Window ends on the newest issue_date in the mirror. It fires at over 1.5x or under 0.5x.

items.a: Zip surge: is one zip getting many backup permits all at once? Rule: A zip's backup permits (generator, battery, solar_battery) in the last 30 days vs its trailing 12-month monthly mean. It fires at over 3x, min 5 permits.

items.q: What does the price spike signal mean?
items.a: Price spike: is Austin power very expensive right now? Rule: LZ_AEN day-ahead or real-time settlement point price in the newest system-wide-prices snapshot. It fires at over $200/MWh.
items.source: store/signals.py RULES; dam_prices, rt_prices (ERCOT system-wide-prices dashboard)

items.q: What does the low reserves signal mean?
items.a: Low reserves: is the grid close to asking people to save power? Rule: Physical responsive capability in the newest daily-prc snapshot (ERCOT conservation threshold). It fires at under 3,000 MW.

items.q: What does the storm alert signal mean?
items.a: Storm alert: is there a weather alert for Travis or Williamson county? Rule: National Weather Service active alerts for Travis (TXC453) and Williamson (TXC491) counties. It fires at any active alert.

items.q: What does the battery do today?
items.a: Plan for 2026-09-26: charge from 8 am to 11 am, discharge from 6 pm to 9 pm. 30% of 39.2 kWh stays for backup. Our plan, not Base's dispatch.
items.computed: Day-ahead plan from grid/earned.py: charge in the 3 cheapest hours, discharge in the 3 priciest hours, one cycle a day, 30% of the 39.2 kWh always kept for the member's backup.

items.q: What did one battery earn for the grid last year?
items.a: About $603 for all of 2025, or $1.65 a day, on real Austin prices. This is a floor: day-ahead prices and one cycle a day only. It is the value to the grid, not a payment to you.
items.source: ERCOT day-ahead price archive (report 13060), Austin zone, 39.2 kWh battery, 30% kept for backup.

items.q: When is the grid under most stress?
items.a: Late afternoon and evening. Texas uses the most power from 5 pm to 6 pm, and Austin prices are highest from 6 pm to 10 pm. Solar fades then while air conditioning is still on.
items.number: Peak load hour ends 6 pm (63,116 MW average); top price hours 6 pm to 10 pm
items.source: ERCOT hourly load 2024-01-01 to 2026-08-31 and day-ahead prices for the Austin zone.
items.computed: SELECT he, AVG(ercot) FROM load_hourly GROUP BY he; SELECT he, AVG(price) FROM dam_prices WHERE point='LZ_AEN' GROUP BY he

items.q: Where does a number come from?
